author: admin

blocks.text: Katti, a Vienna city tour guide and historian, was too sick to record her usual long video. So she brought in her husband, Stefan, for a special episode: an AI-generated video had popped up in her timeline, a thirty-six-minute attempt at “The Complete History of Vienna,” and she wanted to take it apart from a historian’s perspective. “I’m curious whether the person making these videos even watches them,” Stefan said. “I doubt it,” Katti replied.

The channel could produce long videos at suspiciously fast intervals, which made no sense to people who knew how long proper research, scripting, and editing took. They wouldn’t play the whole thing, but they would check the supposedly historical facts. The intro alone was already a problem. “That’s a mighty cool intro, I have to say,” Stefan admitted.

“Looks almost like the United Nations. But look at her,” Katti said, pointing at the screen. “Is that supposed to be Maria Theresa? ” The figure wore a tricorn hat, which was possible—there were portraits of her mother in similar hunting costume—but the woman stood by a palace railing that could have been Schönbrunn, and her face was covered in strange dark spots. Dirt, grime, disease spots, or something that had been digitized from an old, poorly colored photo. “Maybe she’d been hunting and the rifle blew smoke in her face,” Stefan offered. “Honestly, I don’t think that much thought went into it. ”

The gardeners in the background were dressed too dapperly, one of them even wearing a wig. Then a man appeared, supposedly an emperor or nobleman, his outfit completely stained and filthy. “He looks like he rode through a construction site for three days,” Katti said. “That’s terrible. ” Stefan guessed the stains came from some old photograph that had been digitized along with its blemishes.

“Whoever has a better theory, I’m interested,” he said. Then the screen filled with a wild cityscape. Café Landtmann and Café Central sat side by side, a place that did not exist in Vienna. A tram drove through streets that weren’t right. St. Stephen’s Cathedral stood next to buildings that shouldn’t be there. The Hofburg was visible before it should have been finished. There were three towers on a church that should have had two. Everything was a jumbled mix of historical and modern, foreground and background. “I hope nobody assumes a real city looks like this,” Katti said. The narration claimed Vienna was “the city where Mozart, Beethoven, Freud, and Klimt came from. ”

“Mozart is from Salzburg and Beethoven is from Bonn,” Katti pointed out. “They settled in Vienna and built their careers there, but that sentence is phrased wrong. ” Then came the line about a “dynasty change in 1415” determining the course of six centuries. Katti threw up her hands. “What does that even mean?

The Habsburgs ruled the whole time. It was the same dynasty. ” Stefan noticed a street leading directly onto Heldenplatz with no trees in front of it. “You can walk through the Volksgarten and come out, but there are no houses there. That looks like the Kohlmarkt or something, but the perspective is wrong. ”

The part about the Roman camp wasn’t badly told, Katti admitted, but then a map appeared showing Vienna as a completely round, planned city laid out like a star. “Vienna was never like that,” she said. “Never. Does anyone recognize this city? Is it based on a real template, or is the AI making something up? ” The narration mentioned the Babenbergers bringing stability in 918. Another map appeared, labeled with something Katti couldn’t decipher.

“What is ‘Mark Ösenberger’? And what does ‘Tatlist’ mean? ” She knew the Babenbergers were commissioned in 976, and the area described in a 996 contract was colloquially called “Osterherrich. ” But the map showed Upper Austria, almost all of Lower Austria, and even Burgenland, which had been Hungarian territory back then and was a Habsburg sphere of influence much later. “This is what I find totally dangerous about AI,” she said. “Twisting dates, misrepresenting maps. That map is completely wrong. Please don’t believe this.

” Stefan laughed at the man in the corner of the image, who was hammering a stone with the handle of his hammer instead of the head. “He should be hitting it with the solid part. ” “The other guy over there is doing it too,” Katti said. The video claimed Austria was elevated to a duchy in 1155 and Vienna became the residence.

“It was 1156, not 1155,” Katti said. “How do errors like that even happen? Where does the AI get this data, and why doesn’t the creator check even the dates? That’s grossly negligent. ” When the video said Ottokar’s reign ended in 1276 after he submitted to Rudolf of Habsburg, recently elected “German King,” Katti stopped it. “Two mistakes. First, they wouldn’t have called themselves ‘German King’ back then. That’s a later attribution.

‘Deutsch’ was originally an exonym used by people in Italy for the barbarians in the north who didn’t speak Latin. The Holy Roman Empire wasn’t just German territories—it included Italy, Switzerland, Bohemia, the Netherlands, Luxembourg, Belgium. They saw themselves as successors to the Roman emperors, not rulers of a German empire. ” “And second,” Stefan added, “Ottokar didn’t surrender. He died in that battle. ”

“He died in the battle, yes. ” A later segment claimed Frederick III, who had the longest reign of any medieval German king or emperor, preferred living in Wiener Neustadt over Vienna. “That might have been because the Viennese kicked him out,” Katti said. “He didn’t have a choice. ”

The depiction of Frederick showed him with a white beard, but his sarcophagus in St. Stephen’s showed a smooth-faced man. “The portrayals in books always show him clean-shaven. ” The video mentioned Rudolf II preferring Prague, then said Vienna only permanently became the residence under Ferdinand I in the mid-sixteenth century. Katti frowned. “That’s told in a very wild, strange, chronological way. Rudolf comes after Ferdinand, not before.

” The image of the Hofburg had ancient triumphal arches and aqueducts in the middle of the courtyard. “That’s pure fantasy,” she said. “The Schweizerhof never had huge arcades like that. ” In the background, a wall stretched out like the Great Wall of China.

Katti didn’t recognize it. “There’s no wall in Vienna that far outside the city. There are fortifications on Leopoldsberg and Kahlenberg, but they’re small, not huge. ” The narration claimed Hungary had “ceased to exist ten years earlier in the catastrophe of Mohács. ”

“Wait a minute,” Katti said. “Mohács is 1526. The siege of Vienna is 1529. That’s three years, not ten. ” Then the video showed Roman soldiers during a segment about the Ottomans. “What is that doing there? ” Stefan said. “Legionnaires and First World War soldiers in the same scene.

The rifles look modern, the helmets and coats are from the First World War. In 1529 they had muskets and arquebuses. ” The video noted that Emperor Leopold left Vienna during the siege, calling it “historically documented and often forgotten. ” “I don’t understand that statement at all,” Katti said.

“That was normal back then. The emperor didn’t fight at the front line. He shouldn’t stay in a besieged city, because if the city fell and the emperor was captured, that would be absolute defeat. From outside, he can organize resistance and gather troops. Inside a trapped city, he can’t do anything. It was only logical. ” “And it wasn’t just Leopold during the second siege,” Stefan added. “It was the same during the first.

” Katti laughed at the image of Ottoman soldiers digging trenches in peace while Viennese soldiers watched from above. “Totally relaxed. They’re doing it so harmoniously. ” A soldier in the corner looked like he belonged to Napoleon’s army.

“But by now we’ve come to terms with these anachronisms. ” Then came the strangest moment yet. A soldier hit his own comrade on the head with a hammer, having first held a wooden peg. “He hits him on the head with the hammer,” Stefan said. “His own comrade. ”

“He first had a wooden peg in his hand, and then a hammer,” Katti said. The narration claimed the Ottoman defeat at Vienna in ’61 initiated the slow retreat of the Ottoman Empire from Central Europe. “’61? ” Katti said. “1661? 1561? What? That was 1683. Where does that number come from? ”

The map showing the Peace of Karlowitz in 1699 wasn’t as wrong as the others, she admitted, but the documents shown in the video didn’t exist as depicted. Then factory chimneys appeared in the middle of the historical first district. “What are those chimneys doing there? ” she asked. “I don’t know any chimneys in the first district. ” The coffee house segment showed a man sitting outside a café, then cut to the same man sitting inside a carriage.

“He was just in the coffee house a moment ago,” Stefan said. “Yes, now he’s in a carriage. ” A huge fountain appeared, and St. Charles Church stood right in the middle of the city, just before Heldenplatz, with what looked like the Belvedere behind it. “The AI simply stitches elements from Vienna together into one image as if it actually looked like that. ”

But then Katti found a positive point. “They said ‘Empress Maria Theresa. ’” She had spent years pushing back against the claim that Maria Theresa didn’t bear the title of empress alongside her husband. She did, even if she wasn’t crowned. “Okay, great. One fact in this video. ” The video claimed the city had around two hundred thousand inhabitants in the mid-eighteenth century.

Katti clarified: “At the time of Maria Theresa, Vienna had about one hundred thousand. With the suburbs, two hundred thousand, but officially the suburbs weren’t part of Vienna then. Vienna was only as large as the city walls reached—today’s first district, about fifty thousand. ” Mozart appeared, writing notes furiously with two quills, then one. “That’s unusual,” Katti said. “And chronologically it’s odd. He was in Salzburg first, worked for Archbishop Colloredo, broke with him, then went to Vienna. He wasn’t tied to court life—he didn’t get an appointment at the Viennese court until 1786, and even then he remained a freelance artist on the side.
” Then came the evil Beethoven, running angrily through the city, slamming on piano keys. “Why is he so angry? Where is he running to? What did they do to Beethoven? ”

The narration claimed Napoleon dissolved the Holy Roman Empire in 1806. “Stop,” Katti said. “Napoleon didn’t dissolve it. Only the emperor could do that, and that was Emperor Franz. Even if he was allowed to—and legal historians still debate that—he could only resign as emperor. He couldn’t dissolve the empire. ” The doors of the Hofburg were burning in the image. “Why are the doors burning?

” A map labeled “Congress 1815” was illegible and riddled with errors. Saxony appeared twice, drawn all the way to the left and all the way to the right. “That’s not Saxony anymore,” Katti said. “Where is Saxony now? It’s wild. ”

A hand appeared to be giving something from a book. “What is that? Nuts? ” Stefan said. They both laughed. The video showed Franz Joseph scribbling and crossing things out. Then came an image of Parliament with a real person sitting on a horse statue. A carriage drove up the steps, where there was no ramp. “Where is it going? ” Stefan asked. “It’s driving behind the fountain.

” Then came a date: August 1880. A young man from Braunau, rejected twice by the Vienna Art Academy, lived in homeless shelters in the city. “Adolf Hitler spent several years in Vienna between 1908 and 1913,” Katti said. “Why does Hitler come to Vienna in 1880? He wasn’t even born yet. These date errors again. I don’t understand it. ”

The video mentioned a populist mayor named Karl Lueger. The AI pronounced the name strangely, almost like “Karl Liar. ” “Given the statements he sometimes made, that isn’t actually that bad,” Katti said. “Although he wasn’t lying—he was expressing what he thought. But it’s a funny slip of the tongue.

” The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand was followed by a map so distorted that Katti and Stefan could barely stop laughing. “Czechoslovakia, Austriary, Polen, Hungary, Yugoslavia,” Stefan read. “Yugoslavia goes all the way up to the Baltics. What is that? ”

“If you’re going to show a map, show a real one or none at all,” Katti said. “This is madness. ” A man in a coffee shop ate his cigarettes. The Ringstrasse was running through the Kärntner Strasse. There was a DM store next to St. Stephen’s Cathedral. “Why? ” Katti asked.

“Why is the tram going through there? That’s supposed to be the Ringstrasse, but it’s suddenly in the Kärntner Strasse. ” At the time of the Anschluss, Vienna was labeled as a “Gau capital. ” The map showed Switzerland with a strange label. “Maybe someone knows what language that is,” Katti said. “If you know, please write it in the comments. ”

Then came the map of occupied Vienna after the war, and it was wrong in major ways. “The Mühlviertel north of the Danube is the Soviet zone, not the American zone. The French zone is way out west, just a small piece. And the international zone in Vienna—I have no idea what this is supposed to be. ” The signing of the Austrian State Treaty showed diplomats appearing twice, Molotov and Harold Macmillan each shown as two different signatures. “The first and the last,” Stefan said.

“You can recognize the actual signers—John Foster Dulles, Antoine Pinay, Leopold Figl at the bottom, signing in green. But the rest is a mess. ” A map for Austria’s EU accession labeled the country oddly. “Look, it says ‘Polland,’” Katti said. “And down there—what is that? Greece? ”

Stefan laughed. “Dear Floridsdorf and Donaustadt residents, you now live in Eastern Europe. That’s confirmed. ” The map split Austria in two, with a border that began in the middle of Vienna. “What does that even mean? ” Katti asked.

“That doesn’t reflect any reality. ” An image of St. Stephen’s Cathedral showed the cathedral twice, with two naves. “What happened there? ” Stefan said. “It has two cathedrals, and this golden building is in the middle. ”

A statue on the Judenplatz was labeled with the name Ludwig Reiter. “Who is Ludwig Reiter? ” Katti asked. “Who is that? ” The architecture looked more like the Pantheon in Rome. A decapitated eagle statue sat in front of what was supposed to be the entrance to the Hofburg. “What happened to the poor eagle? It has no heads left. ”

The video ended with a chaotic traffic scene heading toward St. Stephen’s Cathedral, the Ringstrasse appearing again, the cathedral somehow outside the Ring, with strange bridges. Stefan turned to Katti. “Well, what do we say to that? ” “AI can definitely be helpful,” Katti said. “But uncontrolled AI is terrible.

Even the smallest details are wrong. The maps are wrong, the descriptions are wrong, the dates are wrong. The guy with the style, the exploding walls—those might be graphics errors, but there is false information in there. I wonder how the script was even created. Someone must have typed ‘create a script for me about the history of Vienna’ and then never checked it. You could look up those dates so quickly, even on Wikipedia. The dates in the video are written correctly there. ” “So where did the AI get the wrong data?

” Stefan asked. “It could be intentional,” Katti said. “Rage baiting, so people get upset and write comments, and the viewership numbers go up. But I don’t think so. These videos appear at far too short intervals. Someone just tells the AI to create scripts about different cities and countries, then produces and posts them quickly, probably just to earn money on YouTube. The longer the videos, the more ad revenue. ” They had watched it only for documentation, to see what content could come out of such videos.

“It has absolutely no added value,” Katti said. “I sometimes like watching AI-generated videos of how a city looked in the past, but you don’t even get that here. The cityscapes are wrong—they don’t look like Vienna and never did. There’s neither that added value nor the claim to tell a complete history, because nothing is complete or correct. So why does this video exist? I don’t understand it. ” Stefan shook his head. “That just wears me out.

” “I’m not against AI in principle,” Katti said. “You can use it in a great way if you feed it correctly and check the results. Someone who knows their stuff would say, ‘Wait, dear AI, we can’t do it like that. ’ But either there’s someone behind these videos who doesn’t know their stuff, or someone who doesn’t care and just wants to produce videos quickly. Neither is good. ”

She asked the viewers to write in the comments if they should analyze another AI video, noting that the one they watched didn’t have many views, but others did—on the Habsburgs, for example, or Austria-Hungary. “Thanks for watching,” Katti said. “Next week, when I’m healthy again, there will be a new long video about a historical figure, well-researched. The script is already written. ” Stefan said his goodbye. “I’m driving to Bree now,” he said, “or taking a quick trip to Eastern Europe—to Floridsdorf. I’ll head out now, and I’ve already prepared my hammer handle for it.
